title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
text:
Every Form 990 has a section where the organization describes its programs in its own words. Part III asks for each major program’s “accomplishments,” and the 990-EZ asks for a “statement of program service accomplishments.” The question invites an organization to say what changed because of its work.
I read what Utah’s charities wrote there. In the filings I could see, most organizations describe what they do. About a third count what they did. About 2 in 100 say what changed.

Here’s what each category looks like. These are paraphrased composites, not quotes from any one filing:

Activities: “Provides after-school tutoring to youth in the community.”
Outputs: “Served 412 students through 3,100 tutoring sessions.”
Outcome: “Of the 412 students, 78% raised their reading score by at least one grade level.”

The outcomes that did appear were concrete: students who graduated or tested at grade level, families who moved into stable housing and stayed housed, participants who found jobs or raised their income, child-welfare cases that closed with children still at home, criminal records cleared, animals adopted. A few organizations reported survey results, such as the share of participants who said a program changed their knowledge or behavior.

title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
section: Size helps with counting, not with outcomes
text:
Size helps with counting, not with outcomes

Larger organizations are more likely to put numbers in their description. Output counting rises from 24% of charities under $100,000 to about 40% of those over $1 million. Outcome reporting barely moves. It’s 2% among charities with $5 million or more in revenue, about the same as at $100,000.
That’s the interesting part. Big organizations have finance staff, grant writers, and often an evaluation contract. They clearly can count. When it comes to the one question Part III invites, what changed, most of them answer the same way a volunteer-run league does.

title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
text:
What it means
For organizations, the gap usually isn’t effort or honesty. Counting outputs is the natural first step, because outputs live in records you already keep: attendance sheets, intake forms, the food bank’s pounds log. Outcomes require something more: deciding in advance what change you’re after, and then checking whether it happened, often after the person has left your program.
For funders and boards, the 990 isn’t where outcomes live, and that’s fine. But if the organization’s own reports look like its 990, with plenty of activity and lots of counts but no result, that’s worth a conversation.

title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
section: What this says about analytics maturity
text:
What this says about analytics maturity
This is the gap between purpose and questions, the first two stages of the maturity framework I use. Nearly every mission statement names a change: healthier kids, stable families, a cleaner river. Few organizations turn that change into a question they can answer with data: Of the families we housed last year, how many are still housed?
Until the question exists, there’s nothing to measure, and no dashboard will fix that. A practical first step: for your largest program, write down one change you expect in the people you serve, how you’d know it happened, and when you’d check. One outcome, tracked consistently, beats ten outputs.

title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
text:
What the data can’t see

Part III is a narrative written for the IRS, not an evaluation report. Many organizations measure outcomes and publish them in annual reports or grant reports instead. This finding is about what organizations choose to put in the public record, not what they know.
Some descriptions continue on Schedule O, which isn’t included here. I excluded descriptions that only said “See Schedule O.”
The 990-EZ leaves less room. Outcome reporting was 2.2% on the full 990 and 0.6% on the 990-EZ.
This covers only organizations that e-file a 990 or 990-EZ. As post #1 showed, most of Utah’s smallest organizations file the 990-N postcard, which has no program description at all.
The outcome count is close to a lower bound. See the method notes below.

title: Utah charities count what they do, not what changes
text:
Method


Data, classification and validation


Organizations: Utah 501(c)(3) public charities in the IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File with a 990 or 990-EZ e-filed for tax years 2021–2024. I used each organization’s most recent return: 3,096 organizations, 1,900 full 990s and 1,196 990-EZs. 94% of the returns are for tax years 2023–2024.
Text: All program-service descriptions on the return (Part III lines 4a–4d on the 990; Part III on the 990-EZ), joined together. Placeholder text (“See Schedule O,” “N/A”) was excluded.
Classification: Three levels, assigned to the highest that applies. Activities only means no quantities. Counts outputs means quantities of service delivered (people, sessions, meals, events, dollars granted); years, grade ranges, ages and section numbers don’t count. Reports an outcome means a specific, observed change for the people or conditions served: graduation, test results, housing or employment placement, measured improvement, a case resolved, an adoption. General claims (“youth gain confidence”) without evidence don’t count, and neither does completing a course.
Validation: I hand-read a random sample of 200 descriptions. A rule-based classifier agreed with the hand labels on 192 (96%). Every description the rules flagged as an outcome (64) was then read and confirmed or rejected, and I read two further keyword sweeps (about 490 descriptions mentioning percentages, surveys, graduation, placement, housing and similar terms) to find outcomes the rules missed. That review found 49 outcome reporters.
Uncertainty: In the hand-read random sample, 6 of 150 charities (4%) reported an outcome. That sample is small (95% interval roughly 1.5%–8.5%), and the full review may have missed some outcomes phrased in unusual ways. The honest summary is between about 2% and 4%: fewer than 1 in 20.
Revenue bands use total revenue on the same return.




The classification rules (Python)

# Outcome patterns (excerpt) — every match was then read by hand
R_PATS = [
  r'\d+%\s*(OF\s+)?(PARTICIPANTS|STUDENTS|CLIENTS|FAMILIES|GRADUATES|...)'
  r'[^.]{0,120}(REPORT|INCREAS|IMPROV|REDUC|GRADUAT|EMPLOY|HOUS|MAINTAIN|...)',
  r'(INCREAS|IMPROV|REDUC|DECREAS|GAIN)\w*\s+(OF|IN|BY)\s+\d',
  r'(GRADUATION|PLACEMENT|RETENTION|PASS|SUCCESS|RECIDIVISM)\s+RATES?',
  r'(ASSESSMENT|EVALUATION|SURVEY|DATA)[^.]{0,80}(INDICAT|SHOW|FOUND)[^.]{0,80}(GAIN|IMPROV|...)',
  r'(WERE ABLE TO|SUCCESSFULLY)\s+(CLOSE|KEEP|OBTAIN|SECURE|FIND|GRADUATE|...)',
]
# Output = any quantity left after removing years, ages, grade ranges, IRC sections, addresses
def classify(text):
    if any(p.search(text) for p in R_PATS): return 'outcome (review)'
    return 'outputs' if NUM.search(NOISE.sub(' ', text)) else 'activities'

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
text:
I’ve been building a database of Utah’s tax-exempt organizations from public IRS data. It starts with the IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File, the list of every organization the IRS recognizes as exempt, and joins it to the IRS index of e-filed Form 990-series returns. With a Utah mailing address as the boundary, that’s 13,072 organizations.
The first thing the data shows is how little of the sector it can see, and that’s by design. Reporting rules are deliberately light for small organizations. One with gross receipts normally under $50,000 files a 990-N e-Postcard, and churches don’t file at all. The trade-off is reasonable: small organizations rarely have an accountant on staff, and together they hold very little of the sector’s money. Even if all 7,389 Utah organizations on the e-Postcard took in the full $50,000, they would total about $370 million, roughly 1% of the $32 billion in revenue the IRS records for Utah exempt organizations.
The other side of that trade-off is that almost no one looks. In fiscal 2025 the IRS examined 889 Form 990, 990-EZ and 990-N returns nationwide, out of about 1.8 million returns filed by tax-exempt organizations, or roughly 1 in 2,000 (IRS Data Book, 2025, Tables 1-2 and 3-5). Since May 2024, Utah no longer registers charities that ask the public for donations.
For a small nonprofit, outside oversight is close to zero, so accountability rests almost entirely on the organization itself: its board, its funders, and its own records. That’s why analytics maturity starts with clean, transparent data, not dashboards. Good records let you show donors what their money did, show the people you serve that you’re delivering, and answer the IRS on the rare day it asks. When no one outside is checking, your own data is how you keep the public’s trust.

Only 2,671 organizations (20%) have e-filed a full Form 990 since 2017. That’s the version that reports revenue and expenses in detail, officers and their pay, grants made, and program accomplishments. Another 1,567 have filed only the short-form 990-EZ, and 1,261 are private foundations filing the 990-PF.
The other 58% have no e-filed information return at all. (That includes 19 organizations whose only e-filing is a 990-T, a tax return on business income rather than an information return.)

text:
Who’s missing, and why
Most of them aren’t gone. The IRS master file records what each organization is required to file, and that explains almost all of the gap:

*The 19 organizations that filed only a 990-T are counted with the filers here, because they have an e-filed record.

The 990-N e-Postcard is how small organizations meet their annual filing requirement. It confirms little more than a name, an address, a principal officer, and that gross receipts are under the limit. It isn’t in the e-file index used here, and it carries no financial detail anyway.
Churches aren’t required to file a 990 of any kind, whatever their size. Many never apply for IRS recognition at all, so the master file undercounts them to begin with.
The 376 organizations required to file that have no e-filed return could be new, late, covered by a group return, or on their way to automatic revocation. That small group deserves its own look.

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
section: Which kinds of organizations are least visible
text:
Which kinds of organizations are least visible

Fraternal societies (84% with no e-filed return) and veterans’ organizations (83%) are the least visible, followed by public charities (65%). Business leagues (38%) and private foundations (10%) are the most visible. Foundations have to file the 990-PF regardless of size.

By mission area, religion (78%), public safety (71%), recreation and sports (65%), and arts and culture (62%) are the least visible. Philanthropy (21%) and housing (46%) are the most visible. One note: “Religion” here is a mission label from the IRS’s NTEE classification, not the church filing status above. Many church-coded organizations have no NTEE code at all, and some religion-coded organizations are charities that do have to file.

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
text:
What it means
For anyone who uses 990 data (funders, researchers, journalists, and consultants like me), the detailed picture covers the larger fifth of the sector. Benchmarks built from Form 990 filings describe organizations big enough to file one: generally those with gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or assets of $500,000 or more. Smaller organizations can use the 990-EZ or, under $50,000, the postcard.
For a small organization, the public record says almost nothing about your work. Your mission, your programs, and the people you serve don’t show up in any dataset someone else can download.

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
section: What this says about analytics maturity
text:
What this says about analytics maturity
In maturity terms, this is the data stage: your own records are the only evidence of your work. It doesn’t require a data warehouse or a dashboard. It requires a habit.
A practical first step: pick three things to record the same way every month (who you served, what you did, and one sign that something changed) and keep them in one place. Organizations that do this can answer a funder’s question, spot a trend, or make a case to their board. Organizations that don’t are invisible twice: once in public data, and again in their own.

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
text:
What the data can’t see

Missing from e-file doesn’t mean defunct. Most of these organizations file the 990-N, which isn’t in the e-file index, or are churches that don’t have to file.
Paper returns aren’t included. E-filing became mandatory for tax years beginning after July 1, 2019, and for the 990-EZ for tax years ending July 31, 2021 or later (IRS). Earlier paper filings don’t appear.
“Utah” means a Utah mailing address on the IRS record. That leaves out organizations headquartered elsewhere that serve Utah, and includes some that only use a Utah address.
About 21% of organizations have no NTEE mission code, so the mission-area breakdown covers the rest plus a “No NTEE code” bar.

title: Most of Utah’s nonprofit sector is invisible in public data
text:
Method


Data and classification


Organizations: IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File, Utah extract (eo_ut.csv), retrieved September 7, 2026. All exempt subsections; 87% are 501(c)(3).
Filings: IRS Form 990 e-file indexes, 2017–2026 (index_<year>.csv). That’s 34,584 filings matched to 5,518 Utah EINs.
Cross-check: the IRS reports 12,569 tax-exempt organization returns filed in Utah in fiscal 2025 (IRS Data Book, 2025, Table 1-3), in line with the 13,072 organizations in the master file.
Return types: the index uses seven codes. Older index files label some returns 990O, 990EO, and 990PR; the document locator number (DLN) prefix confirms these are a full 990, a 990-EZ, and a 990-PF. 990T is the unrelated business income tax return.
Classification: each organization is counted once, by the most complete return it has e-filed: full 990, then 990-PF, then 990-EZ, then 990-T only, then none.
Why not revenue size? The master file shows $0 or no revenue for 72% of organizations, including nearly all non-filers, because it takes revenue from filed returns. The filing-requirement code is the better size signal.

title: Services
section: Keep critical organizational knowledge from walking out the door.
text:
Keep critical organizational knowledge from walking out the door.
Organizations accumulate enormous amounts of knowledge about how work actually gets done: procedures, exceptions, workarounds, relationships, decision rules, historical context, reporting requirements, data definitions, and lessons learned. Much of that knowledge is never formally documented.
It lives in the heads of experienced employees, scattered files, email threads, spreadsheets, shared drives, old procedure manuals, and systems that only a few people fully understand. When experienced staff leave, retire, change roles, or become unavailable, organizations can lose years of institutional knowledge.
I help organizations capture that knowledge, turn it into structured and maintainable documentation, and build AI-assisted knowledge systems that make it easier for staff to find and use what the organization already knows.


From undocumented work to institutional memory
This work combines process analysis, knowledge management, documentation, data architecture, and practical AI. The goal is not simply to install an AI chatbot. The goal is to create an organizational memory system that people can trust.
Depending on the organization, that can include:

Interviewing subject-matter experts and experienced staff
Documenting workflows and business processes
Creating and standardizing standard operating procedures (SOPs)
Identifying undocumented decision rules, exceptions, and workarounds
Inventorying manuals, policies, reports, spreadsheets, shared files, and reference materials
Defining terminology, data definitions, roles, responsibilities, and dependencies
Mapping relationships between processes, systems, people, policies, data, and information
Identifying knowledge concentrated in one person or team
Establishing processes for keeping documentation current
Building AI-assisted interfaces that let employees search and interact with organizational knowledge



Capabilities

Institutional knowledge assessment
Workflow discovery and process mapping
SOP development and standardization
Knowledge-risk and continuity assessment
Knowledge architecture and metadata design
Searchable internal knowledge bases
AI knowledge assistants and semantic search
Source-linked retrieval systems
Documentation governance and handoff
Retirement, succession, and transition knowledge capture




A practical engagement model
1. Knowledge discovery
We begin by understanding where important organizational knowledge currently lives. This can involve staff interviews, review of existing documentation, observation of recurring processes, analysis of shared drives or knowledge repositories, and identification of systems and data sources involved in the work.
The objective is to distinguish between what is already documented, what is outdated, what exists only informally, and what represents a significant continuity risk.
2. Workflow mapping
Important recurring processes are mapped from beginning to end. The objective is to document how the work actually happens—not merely the ideal workflow shown in a policy manual.
Trigger → Inputs → People → Decisions → Systems → Outputs → Exceptions → Handoff
This often exposes duplicated work, undocumented dependencies, manual steps, bottlenecks, and places where only one person knows what to do.
3. SOP and documentation development
Critical workflows are converted into clear, maintainable documentation. Depending on the process, this may include standard operating procedures, process maps, checklists, decision trees, roles and responsibilities, data definitions, system instructions, exception handling, reporting procedures, business rules, source documentation, and historical context explaining why important practices exist.
Documentation is designed for actual use rather than simply satisfying a documentation requirement.
4. Knowledge architecture
The resulting information is organized so that people—and AI systems—can retrieve it reliably. Rather than accumulating another folder full of documents, we establish a structure connecting related information.
Process ↔︎ SOP ↔︎ Role ↔︎ System ↔︎ Data ↔︎ Policy ↔︎ Decision ↔︎ Source
For some organizations, a conventional document repository with strong metadata may be sufficient. More complex environments may benefit from structured databases, knowledge graphs, semantic search, or retrieval systems that preserve relationships between different kinds of organizational knowledge. The technology should fit the problem rather than the other way around.
5. AI-assisted organizational knowledge
Once the underlying knowledge is documented and structured, AI can provide a much more useful interface to it. Employees might ask:

How do I prepare the quarterly report?
Who is responsible for approving this?
What happens if the normal process fails?
Where does this number come from?
Why do we calculate this measure this way?
Which SOP applies to this situation?
What systems are affected if this process changes?

The system can retrieve relevant organizational knowledge and point employees back to the underlying documentation and authoritative sources. This is fundamentally different from giving employees a general-purpose AI tool and hoping it understands the organization.


Institutional knowledge at risk
One particularly valuable application is succession and continuity planning. An experienced employee who has performed a function for ten or twenty years may know hundreds of things that were never written down: which exceptions occur regularly, why a spreadsheet is structured a certain way, which data sources can be trusted, what needs to happen before an annual process begins, who needs to be consulted, which shortcuts create problems later, why a policy was interpreted a particular way, and what previous attempts did not work.
A structured knowledge-transfer engagement can capture that information before a retirement, departure, reorganization, or leadership transition. Instead of asking an employee to “write down everything you know,” I use interviews, workflow analysis, document review, and structured knowledge capture to uncover what another person would actually need to perform the work.


Possible deliverables

Knowledge inventory: a map of where critical organizational knowledge currently resides
Knowledge-risk assessment: identification of functions that depend heavily on undocumented individual knowledge
Workflow maps: visual representations of how important organizational processes actually operate
Standard operating procedures: consistent, usable documentation for recurring work
Knowledge architecture: a structure connecting procedures, policies, systems, data, roles, decisions, and supporting documentation
Searchable knowledge base: a centralized repository designed around how employees actually look for information
AI knowledge assistant: a secure conversational interface for finding and understanding internal organizational knowledge
Source-linked answers: AI responses that point employees back to authoritative internal documentation
Documentation governance: ownership, review, change tracking, and maintenance processes
Transition knowledge capture: focused documentation and interviews for retiring, departing, or transitioning employees



Where this creates value
This work is particularly useful when a long-tenured employee is preparing to retire, an organization has experienced turnover, important processes depend on one or two people, new employees take too long to learn how things work, staff repeatedly ask the same operational questions, SOPs are missing or outdated, documentation is scattered across systems, processes have evolved informally, leadership is preparing for succession or restructuring, or an organization wants to use AI internally but does not yet have its knowledge organized well enough to do so reliably.


AI comes last, not first.
A chatbot sitting on top of poorly organized information does not solve an institutional knowledge problem. The underlying work is understanding the organization: its people, processes, information, decisions, systems, and history.
Once that foundation exists, AI can make institutional knowledge dramatically easier to access.
Capture the knowledge. Structure it. Document it. Connect it. Then use AI to make it useful.

title: Services
text:
Institutional Knowledge Risk Assessment
For organizations that want a smaller starting point, I offer a focused assessment designed to identify where important knowledge is vulnerable before committing to a larger documentation or technology project.
A typical assessment can include interviews with 4–8 key staff, an inventory of critical workflows and existing documentation, identification of single points of knowledge failure, a risk assessment of processes that depend on undocumented expertise, and a prioritized roadmap for documentation, knowledge transfer, and potential AI-enabled access.
The assessment provides a practical path from knowledge risk → workflow documentation → SOP development → knowledge architecture → AI knowledge system.
